screens.title: Deploying Android Apps to the Google Play Store
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn the full workflow for preparing and publishing an Android app on Google Play. We begin by clarifying why app signing exists and why your keystore is the single most important file for future updates. Then you'll see how to create a keystore, integrate it into your project's build configuration, and build a signed Android App Bundle — Google’s preferred format. We will also walk through the Play Console tasks: creating a store listing, uploading assets and screenshots, and choosing appropriate release tracks for testing and gradual rollouts. I’ll point out common mistakes that lead to rejections and the practical steps to avoid them, such as backing up keys and answering the content rating questionnaire accurately. Throughout, I’ll give concrete examples you can reproduce in Android Studio and practical checks you should perform before uploading a release. By the end you will understand both the technical signing steps and the release management options that minimize risk when you publish an update.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Deploying Android Apps
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Deploying Android Apps to the Google Play Store

Learn signing, build configuration, App Bundles, Play Console listings, testing tracks, and staged rollouts to publish safely.

In this lesson: signing → build → release
Signing
Create and protect a keystore that identifies your app author and enables updates.
Build
Generate a signed Android App Bundle (AAB) for Play to optimize APKs per device.
Release
Use internal, closed, open testing and staged rollouts to manage risk during distribution.
Explore Key Topics
Keystore Safety

Back up your keystore and store passwords securely; losing them blocks updates.

App Bundle (AAB)

AAB lets Play produce optimized APKs, reducing download size for users.

Release Tracks

Use internal, closed, open testing to validate quality before production rollout.

Visual Overview
Keystore → Signed AAB → Play Console

This flow ensures your app is identifiable, securely signed, and distributed via Play's optimized channels.

Testing Tracks

Internal for fast checks, closed for targeted beta groups, open for broad beta, and staged rollout for controlled production release.

Key Takeaway

Protect your keystore, prefer AAB for Play, and use testing tracks to catch issues before exposing real users to a change.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your practice on the technical skills and decision points that matter when publishing on Google Play. First, you will understand why app signing exists and how the keystore secures updates; this matters because signing provides identity and update integrity. Second, you will be able to generate a keystore and configure Android Studio or Gradle to produce signed release builds. You will practice the signing wizard and the build configuration so your release process becomes repeatable. Third, you'll learn how to navigate the Play Console to create a store listing, upload required assets, and complete metadata and rating questionnaires to meet review requirements. Fourth, you will use release tracks effectively: running internal or closed tests, opening broader beta tests, and performing staged production rollouts to reduce risk. Each objective includes a short practice step and a competency milestone so you can verify your progress. Keeping these skills in mind helps you avoid common failures like losing a keystore, missing required store assets, or skipping staged rollout checks.

screens.title: Why App Signing Matters
screens.narratorSegment: App signing is the process of applying a cryptographic signature to your Android application using a private key stored in a keystore. This signature tells Android and Google Play who authored the app and ensures that future updates are signed by the same developer. Practically, signing enforces integrity: if an update is signed with a different key, the Android system will reject it as potentially malicious. A concrete example: if you publish your first release with a keystore named my_app. jks and then lose that file, any new build you sign with a different keystore will not match the original signature, and Google Play will reject the update. A common misconception is that the keystore is only needed for the first release; in reality it is needed every time you update the app. Another misconception is that Play will replace your key automatically — this is false unless you explicitly enroll in Play App Signing and follow its key management flow, which still requires careful handling. The takeaway is simple: the keystore is the app's identity, and protecting it with secure backups and strong passwords is essential to keep the ability to publish updates.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Why App Signing Matters
Core Concept

Why App Signing Matters

Digital signatures provide identity and update integrity. Treat the keystore as your release keyring.

Definition

App signing uses a private key in a keystore to create a signature that proves an app's origin and secures updates.

Concrete Example

If your first release uses my_app.jks, all future updates must be signed with that same key. If it’s lost, you cannot upload matching updates.

Misconception

Some think Play replaces developer keys automatically. Only enroll in Play App Signing deliberately and follow its instructions; otherwise your keystore remains authoritative.

Analogy

Think of the keystore as a safe deposit box containing your signature stamp. Losing it is like losing the stamp used to sign official releases.

Key Takeaway

Protect the keystore and its passwords; losing them prevents valid updates.

Common Mistake

Storing the keystore only inside the project repository without an external backup.

screens.title: Generating a Keystore (keytool & Android Studio)
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a keystore can be done with the keytool command-line utility or through Android Studio’s Generate Signed Bundle / APK wizard. The essential data you provide are the keystore file path, a strong keystore password, a key alias, and a key password. You will also fill in certificate metadata like your name, organization, and country code and set key validity to a long period such as 25 years so it remains valid across many releases. A practical example: run keytool to create a keystore or open the wizard in Android Studio and choose Create new, point the keystore path to a safe external folder, enter a unique alias like my_app_key, and set passwords you store in a secure password manager. A common misconception is that short validity is safe; instead choose long validity to avoid expiration issues. Also do not commit the keystore or passwords to source control. The process ends by backing up the. jks to secure storage and recording the path and credentials, which ensures you can sign future updates. Generating a Keystore (keytool & Android Studio) means generate a .jks with a long validity, strong passwords, and secure off-project backups.. In practical terms, create a secure .jks and choose robust passwords and validity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Generating a Keystore
Process Flow

Generate a Keystore

Choose a secure path, a long validity period, and strong passwords. Never commit keys to source control.

Step 1: Decide location

Store the .jks outside the project, on an encrypted drive or secure cloud backup.

Step 2: Create key

Use Android Studio wizard or keytool; record alias and passwords in a password manager.

Step 3: Backup

Keep multiple secure backups and never share passwords in plain channels.

Command-line Example
keytool -genkeypair -v -keystore my_app.jks -alias my_app_key -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 9125
Concrete Example

Use alias my_app_key, set validity to 25 years (about 9125 days), and store the .jks in a backed-up folder outside the repository.

Common Mistake

Choosing short validity or committing the keystore to source control; both risk future update ability or key exposure.

screens.title: Configuring build.gradle for Signing
screens.narratorSegment: After you create a keystore, configure your module-level build. gradle to reference it so Gradle can sign release builds automatically. The signingConfigs block contains the keystore file path, store password, key alias, and key password. Then attach the signingConfig to the release build type. A concrete example is shown in the code snippet; adapt paths and secrets to your environment and avoid storing raw passwords in source control. One common contrast: developers sometimes put signing data in plain text in the gradle file for convenience. A safer practice is to read sensitive values from a secure properties file excluded from version control or from environment variables. A misconception is that Gradle will ignore incorrect signing configuration; instead it will fail the release build, which is helpful because it prevents accidental unsigned releases. The final step is to run Build → Generate Signed Bundle / APK in Android Studio or run a Gradle assembleRelease to verify that a signed AAB is produced. Configuring build.gradle for Signing means place signingconfigs in module build.gradle and attach to release builds; avoid committing secrets to version control.. In practical terms, add signingconfigs and reference the keystore for automated release builds. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Configuring build.gradle
Definition

Configure Gradle Signing

Reference your keystore so Gradle signs release builds automatically, and keep secrets out of version control.

Safer Practice

Store passwords in a gradle.properties file excluded from git, or use environment variables for CI systems.

Key Takeaway

A correct signing config prevents unsigned releases and supports reproducible builds.

Example build.gradle snippet
android {
    ...
    signingConfigs {
        release {
            storeFile file("your_keystore_name.jks") // Path to your keystore
            storePassword "your_store_password"
            keyAlias "your_key_alias"
            keyPassword "your_key_password"
        }
    }
    buildTypes {
        release {
            signingConfig signingConfigs.release
            minifyEnabled true
            proguardFiles getDefaultProguardFile('proguard-android-optimize.txt'), 'proguard-rules.pro'
        }
    }
}
Note: Replace quoted passwords with secure lookups in real projects. This snippet shows the structure Gradle expects.

screens.title: Building a Signed Android App Bundle (AAB)
screens.narratorSegment: An Android App Bundle packages all compiled code and resources but defers APK generation to Google Play. Building a signed AAB in Android Studio is done through Build → Generate Signed Bundle / APK, selecting Android App Bundle, choosing your module and signing configuration, and finishing the build. The important difference is that Play will then generate optimized device-specific APKs for various screen densities, C P U architectures, and language splits, which reduces download size for end users. A concrete example: you build a single signed myapp. aab and upload it to Play; Play produces tailored APKs so an ARM64 phone downloads only the code and resources it needs instead of the entire universal APK. A misconception is that AAB removes the need for signing; it does not. You still sign the AAB with your keystore before upload. Also note that if you need to distribute APKs outside Play or use a custom installer, you might still produce APKs, but for Play publishing AAB is recommended. Building a Signed Android App Bundle (AAB) means build a signed aab for play so google can create optimized apks for different devices, improving download size and install efficiency.. In practical terms, generate an aab in android studio and understand play's apk generation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Building a Signed AAB
Process

Build a Signed Android App Bundle

Use Android Studio’s Generate Signed Bundle / APK wizard, choose AAB, select your signing config, and finish to create a signed .aab for Play.

Why AAB?

Play creates optimized APKs per device configuration, reducing download and install size for users.

Concrete Example

Upload myapp.aab to Play and Play produces smaller APKs for arm64 devices that exclude unnecessary binaries and resources.

Android Studio Steps
  1. Select Build → Generate Signed Bundle / APK
  2. Choose Android App Bundle and module
  3. Select signing configuration and finish build
Key Takeaway

AAB is the recommended Play publishing format because it enables smaller, optimized APKs at install time.

Misconception

AAB eliminates signing — incorrect. You must sign the AAB before upload using your keystore.

screens.title: AAB vs APK — When to Use Each
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between AAB and APK helps you choose the right distribution method. The Android App Bundle contains all compiled code and resources and lets Google Play generate optimized APKs per device. This results in smaller downloads and is preferred for Play distribution. An APK is a ready-to-install package that you can sign and distribute directly to devices or through alternate stores. A concrete scenario: if you publish via Google Play, prefer a signed AAB so Play can tailor APKs; if you need to provide a direct download or sideload an internal build, generate an APK. A common misconception is that AAB prevents side-loading entirely; AAB is mainly a Play publishing format — if side-loading is required, produce signed APKs. Also note that some distribution channels may require an APK. The key takeaway is to publish AABs to Play for better user experience and produce APKs only when the release channel requires them or for local testing where direct APK installation is necessary. AAB vs APK — When to Use Each means use aab for play to get optimized apks; use apk for direct distribution or sideloading when needed.. In practical terms, trade-offs between android app bundles and apks for distribution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › AAB vs APK
Comparison

AAB vs APK

Android App Bundle (AAB)

Upload to Play; Play generates optimized APKs per device, reducing download size and improving installs.

APK

Direct install package; useful for sideloading, internal distribution, or non-Play stores.

Decision Flow
  1. Publishing to Google Play → prefer AAB.
  2. Need sideloading or alternate store → produce signed APK.
  3. Testing internal installs → APK simplifies direct device installs.
Key Takeaway

For Play, AAB is recommended. Use APK when distribution demands a single installable artifact.

screens.title: Preparing Your Play Store Listing and Assets
screens.narratorSegment: Preparing a complete Play Store listing is as important as signing. A good store listing helps users find and understand your app. Required items include the app name, default language, high-quality icon, feature graphic, and screenshots for phone and tablet sizes. You will also write a short description to summarize the app and a full description to explain features and benefits. Additionally, complete the content rating questionnaire to avoid policy or age-targeting misclassification. A practical example: choose three phone screenshots that highlight core flows, one 7-inch tablet screenshot, and one 10-inch tablet screenshot if your app supports tablets. Ensure images meet Play’s size and format requirements. A common error is submitting placeholder or low-resolution screenshots; reviewers often flag poor assets or mismatched content. The takeaway is to treat store metadata and visuals as part of quality control: accurate, compelling assets reduce rejection risk and improve discoverability. In practical terms, store listing, icons, feature graphics, screenshots, descriptions, and rating form. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Preparing Play Store Listing

Store Listing Essentials

Accurate metadata and polished assets reduce rejection risk and increase installs.

Required Items
  • App name and default language
  • App icon and feature graphic
  • Screenshots for phone, 7" and 10" tablets
  • Short and full descriptions
  • Content rating questionnaire
Practical Tip

Use real app flows for screenshots and keep promotional text truthful to avoid policy violations.

Asset Examples
Phone screenshots (3) — highlight sign-in, home, and a key feature.
Tablet screenshot (7") — show layout adapted for larger screen.
Feature graphic — used in Play Store promotion.
App icon — high resolution and centered composition.
Key Takeaway

Prepare accurate and high-quality assets before upload to increase approval chances and user trust.

screens.title: Google Play Console Release Tracks
screens.narratorSegment: Google Play Console provides release tracks that let you control who receives builds and when. Internal testing distributes to up to 100 trusted testers for quick verification. Closed testing expands to invited groups for broader feedback while still limiting exposure. Open testing publishes a beta listing on Play that anyone can join, letting you collect large-scale feedback. Production is the live channel for public users. A powerful feature inside production is a staged rollout, where you increase exposure by percentage — for example releasing to five percent of users, monitoring crash rates and feedback, and then moving to ten and beyond. A concrete use case: run an internal build to confirm no obvious crashes, use closed testing to exercise edge cases with QA and beta users, then perform a staged rollout in production to catch issues at small scale before a full release. A common misconception is to skip testing tracks and release straight to production; this increases the chance of widespread crashes and negative ratings. The takeaway: use testing tracks and staged rollouts to reduce risk and gather iterative feedback.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Release Tracks
Core Concept

Release Tracks and Staged Rollout

Manage distribution with internal, closed, open testing and staged production rollouts to limit exposure while testing.

Internal testing

Fast distribution to a small, trusted set of testers (up to 100) for quick smoke tests.

Closed testing

Invite groups such as QA or beta users for broader coverage and targeted feedback.

Open testing

Publish a public beta on Play to gather large-scale feedback before production.

Staged Rollout

Deploy to a small percentage of your production users, monitor crashes and feedback, then increase the percentage gradually.

Concrete Example

Start with a 5% rollout, check stability metrics and reviews, then move to 25% and finally 100% when confident.

Common Mistake

Releasing directly to 100% production without staged rollouts increases the blast radius if something goes wrong.

screens.title: Uploading Your AAB and Managing Releases
screens.narratorSegment: Uploading your signed AAB to the Play Console is a multi-step process that includes creating a new application record, completing metadata and assets, and then creating a release for a chosen track. After logging into the Play Console, create an app and set the default language and app name. Complete the store listing fields and content rating. Then go to the Release section, choose the desired track — internal, closed, open, or production — and upload your signed. aab file. Provide release notes that explain what testers or users should verify and use the review checklist to ensure policy compliance. A practical example: upload an AAB to the internal track with release notes like “Internal test: verify login and payment flows,” then add testers by email list. After a successful internal test, move the same build to a closed track for a larger group or promote to production with a staged rollout. A misconception is that testing tracks automatically publish metadata; you still need to complete store listing and rating forms before a production rollout. The key takeaway is to follow the upload checklist, provide clear release notes, and choose the right track to minimize risk.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Uploading Your AAB

Upload and Release

Create a release, upload the signed AAB, add release notes, and choose the testing track or production rollout.

Step-by-step
  1. Create app record and complete store listing
  2. Go to Release section, select track
  3. Upload .aab, add release notes, and publish to testers or staged production
Concrete Example

Upload to internal testing with notes: "Verify login, onboarding, and crash-free startup" and invite QA testers via email.

Review Checklist
  • Store assets complete and accurate
  • Content rating questionnaire filled
  • Privacy policy URL and permissions documented if required
Key Takeaway

Provide clear release notes and follow the Play checklist to speed review and avoid rejections.

Common Mistake

Uploading a build without completing store metadata or rating questionnaire, which can delay or block release.

screens.title: Common Reasons for Rejection and How to Fix Them
screens.narratorSegment: Google’s review focuses on policy compliance, app functionality, and truthful content. Common rejection reasons include missing or inadequate privacy policies when accessing sensitive data, requesting unnecessary permissions, misleading store descriptions or promotional assets, and crashes or broken functionality during review testing. To prevent these, ensure a clear privacy policy URL is present if your app accesses personal data, request only the permissions required for core features, and thoroughly test the app in internal and closed tests for crashes and edge cases. If rejected, Google Play provides feedback; fix the specific issues, rebuild a signed AAB, and resubmit. A concrete example: if the review flags an unnecessary permission for reading contacts, remove or justify that permission and demonstrate in your resubmission notes why the change satisfies policy. A misconception is that rejections are final; they are not—you can correct issues and resubmit. The takeaway: design your app and store listing with review criteria in mind, test thoroughly before upload, and treat rejection feedback as actionable instructions rather than punishment. Common Reasons for Rejection and How to Fix Them means address privacy, permissions, accurate metadata, and functional stability before upload to avoid rejections and speed approval.. In practical terms, policy, permissions, privacy, crashes, misleading content — prevention and remediation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Reasons for Rejection

Common Rejection Reasons

Review checks focus on privacy, requested permissions, functionality and accuracy of the store listing.

Privacy & Permissions

Provide a privacy policy when accessing personal data and request only necessary permissions.

Functionality

Fix crashes, broken features, or behavior that fails during review testing before resubmitting.

Misleading Content

Ensure descriptions and screenshots truthfully represent the app’s experience.

Concrete Fix Example

If the review flags an unnecessary contact permission, remove the permission or explain why it’s required and show how user consent is obtained.

Key Takeaway

Treat rejection feedback as a checklist: fix, rebuild a signed AAB, and resubmit with notes explaining the changes.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn the full workflow for preparing and publishing an Android app on Google Play. We begin by clarifying why app signing exists and why your keystore is the single most important file for future updates. Then you'll see how to create a keystore, integrate it into your project's build configuration, and build a signed Android App Bundle — Google’s preferred format. We will also walk through the Play Console tasks: creating a store listing, uploading assets and screenshots, and choosing appropriate release tracks for testing and gradual rollouts. I’ll point out common mistakes that lead to rejections and the practical steps to avoid them, such as backing up keys and answering the content rating questionnaire accurately. Throughout, I’ll give concrete examples you can reproduce in Android Studio and practical checks you should perform before uploading a release. By the end you will understand both the technical signing steps and the release management options that minimize risk when you publish an update.

These objectives focus your practice on the technical skills and decision points that matter when publishing on Google Play. First, you will understand why app signing exists and how the keystore secures updates; this matters because signing provides identity and update integrity. Second, you will be able to generate a keystore and configure Android Studio or Gradle to produce signed release builds. You will practice the signing wizard and the build configuration so your release process becomes repeatable. Third, you'll learn how to navigate the Play Console to create a store listing, upload required assets, and complete metadata and rating questionnaires to meet review requirements. Fourth, you will use release tracks effectively: running internal or closed tests, opening broader beta tests, and performing staged production rollouts to reduce risk. Each objective includes a short practice step and a competency milestone so you can verify your progress. Keeping these skills in mind helps you avoid common failures like losing a keystore, missing required store assets, or skipping staged rollout checks.

This second objectives slide focuses on testing and review readiness—skills you will apply in the hands-on activity. You will learn how to generate a signed Android App Bundle in Android Studio, record the location of the. aab file, and capture screenshots that demonstrate successful signing. We'll emphasize two practical safeguards: pick a long validity period and back up the keystore in a secure location outside the project folder. You will also practice choosing the right testing channel: use internal testing for quick builds with a small group, closed testing to broaden coverage with invited testers, and open testing to expose a beta to a large audience while still keeping the release non-production. Finally, you will perform a staged rollout to a percentage of your live users and monitor crash reports and feedback. These actions reduce the chance of poor releases and are easy to rehearse on a single app project in Android Studio.

App signing is the process of applying a cryptographic signature to your Android application using a private key stored in a keystore. This signature tells Android and Google Play who authored the app and ensures that future updates are signed by the same developer. Practically, signing enforces integrity: if an update is signed with a different key, the Android system will reject it as potentially malicious. A concrete example: if you publish your first release with a keystore named my_app. jks and then lose that file, any new build you sign with a different keystore will not match the original signature, and Google Play will reject the update. A common misconception is that the keystore is only needed for the first release; in reality it is needed every time you update the app. Another misconception is that Play will replace your key automatically — this is false unless you explicitly enroll in Play App Signing and follow its key management flow, which still requires careful handling. The takeaway is simple: the keystore is the app's identity, and protecting it with secure backups and strong passwords is essential to keep the ability to publish updates.

Creating a keystore can be done with the keytool command-line utility or through Android Studio’s Generate Signed Bundle / APK wizard. The essential data you provide are the keystore file path, a strong keystore password, a key alias, and a key password. You will also fill in certificate metadata like your name, organization, and country code and set key validity to a long period such as 25 years so it remains valid across many releases. A practical example: run keytool to create a keystore or open the wizard in Android Studio and choose Create new, point the keystore path to a safe external folder, enter a unique alias like my_app_key, and set passwords you store in a secure password manager. A common misconception is that short validity is safe; instead choose long validity to avoid expiration issues. Also do not commit the keystore or passwords to source control. The process ends by backing up the. jks to secure storage and recording the path and credentials, which ensures you can sign future updates. Generating a Keystore (keytool & Android Studio) means generate a .jks with a long validity, strong passwords, and secure off-project backups.. In practical terms, create a secure .jks and choose robust passwords and validity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

After you create a keystore, configure your module-level build. gradle to reference it so Gradle can sign release builds automatically. The signingConfigs block contains the keystore file path, store password, key alias, and key password. Then attach the signingConfig to the release build type. A concrete example is shown in the code snippet; adapt paths and secrets to your environment and avoid storing raw passwords in source control. One common contrast: developers sometimes put signing data in plain text in the gradle file for convenience. A safer practice is to read sensitive values from a secure properties file excluded from version control or from environment variables. A misconception is that Gradle will ignore incorrect signing configuration; instead it will fail the release build, which is helpful because it prevents accidental unsigned releases. The final step is to run Build → Generate Signed Bundle / APK in Android Studio or run a Gradle assembleRelease to verify that a signed AAB is produced. Configuring build.gradle for Signing means place signingconfigs in module build.gradle and attach to release builds; avoid committing secrets to version control.. In practical terms, add signingconfigs and reference the keystore for automated release builds. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An Android App Bundle packages all compiled code and resources but defers APK generation to Google Play. Building a signed AAB in Android Studio is done through Build → Generate Signed Bundle / APK, selecting Android App Bundle, choosing your module and signing configuration, and finishing the build. The important difference is that Play will then generate optimized device-specific APKs for various screen densities, C P U architectures, and language splits, which reduces download size for end users. A concrete example: you build a single signed myapp. aab and upload it to Play; Play produces tailored APKs so an ARM64 phone downloads only the code and resources it needs instead of the entire universal APK. The Android App Bundle contains all compiled code and resources and lets Google Play generate optimized APKs per device. This results in smaller downloads and is preferred for Play distribution. An APK is a ready-to-install package that you can sign and distribute directly to devices or through alternate stores. A concrete scenario: if you publish via Google Play, prefer a signed AAB so Play can tailor APKs; if you need to provide a direct download or sideload an internal build, generate an APK.
